title: hw-tuning-gpu-clock-power-kernel-scheduling-draft
body:
Purpose:
This note captures early experiments and recommended knobs for hardware-specific tuning of Redwood's serving runtime. Focus is GPU clocking and power limits, kernel selection heuristics, scheduler placement, and KV cache placement/eviction behavior across four target SKUs: NVIDIA A100, NVIDIA H100, NVIDIA L4, and AMD MI300. This is a working draft: numbers are qualitative and guidance should be validated with our microbench harness for each workload.

Context and constraints:
- Objective: minimize end-to-end p95 latency and per-token cost while maintaining model quality and reliability.
- Workloads: small chat models (context <= 2k tokens), long-context LLMs (16k-64k), embedding-only (stateless) workloads, and high-QPS short-generation workloads.
- Constraints: multi-tenant Dedicated clusters; some nodes run mixed models. We prefer automated policies over manual per-node settings where possible.

General principles (applies to all GPUs):
- Prefer inner-loop kernel strategies that maximize throughput on the primary compute precision (bf16 preferred when model supports it).
- Favor keeping KV cache resident on local HBM whenever possible; only spill to host when unavoidable.
- Use workload-aware batching (dynamic batching with latency SLO headroom) instead of fixed large batches.
- Power-clocking tradeoffs: small increases in sustained GPU clocks can reduce latency variance; aggressive power caps reduce tail throughput and increase latency variance. Test with representative prompts.

Microbenchmark checklist (mandatory before changing knobs on production pool):
- perf/latency script: run 1, 5, 50, 200 concurrent clients with synthetic tokens per-request matching target workload.
- memory-pressure script: warm model, then create KV cache at target context size and allocate additional tensors to quantify spill behavior.
- kernel-selection trace: collect kernel launch histogram and percent time spent in GEMM/TMA/softmax paths.
- energy/power trace: collect nvidia-smi/rocm-smi samples at 1s cadence + host-level power when available.

Per-SKU notes and recommended starting knobs:
1) NVIDIA A100 (40/80GB HBM2e)
- Role: balanced throughput node; strong for mixed batch sizes and popular baseline for Dedicated.
- Clocking: prefer running at a sustained clocks policy (P-state) using persistence mode + locked application clocks where available. For 40GB A100, a conservative application-clocks pair reduces frequency oscillation; start with a medium boost target rather than maximum to avoid thermal throttling under sustained multitenant load.
- Power limit: set at ~90% of default TDP for consolidation clusters to save power with minimal perf loss. Measure: expect ~3-10% throughput drop depending on kernel mix.
- Kernel selection: prefer cuBLAS/CUTLASS fp16/bf16 kernels, ensure use of tensor-core fused-kernels for matmuls. Disable experimental kernels that increase register pressure for long context models.
- Scheduling: group latency-sensitive jobs on a subset of cards with higher application clocks. Use affinity rules to prefer A100 for medium-to-large batch throughput.
- KV cache: store full KV in HBM. If context > available HBM for multi-tenant, use shard-on-device across multiple GPUs rather than spilling to host; if host spill is unavoidable, use page-locked host pinned memory to reduce transfer overhead.

2) NVIDIA H100 (Hopper, HBM3)
- Role: lowest-latency, highest peak throughput for transformer ops, best for latency-sensitive tails and very large models.
- Clocking: H100 benefits from sustained high clocks but is sensitive to thermal headroom. Use sustained high P-state with careful thermal monitoring. Consider boosting PCIe/NVLink awake policies to reduce warm-up latency.
- Power limit: conservative defaults near 95-100% if single-tenant; for multi-tenant, experiment with 90% but validate p95 impact. Small power caps can cause larger p95 regressions on H100 than A100 due to power-to-frequency scaling.
- Kernel selection: prefer cuBLASLt + auto-tuned kernels that target WMMA/Xmma paths and use split-K for large matmuls. Enable cuDNN/Hopper-specialized fused attention where it improves latency.
- Scheduling: pin latency-SLO traffic to H100; do not co-locate heavy background batch jobs unless they are throttled. Use preemptible lower-priority queues for batch work and schedule with immediate fallback to hosted API if contention.
- KV cache: strongly prefer keep-resident on HBM3; H100's larger memory bandwidth favors keeping KV local. For multi-GPU sharded KV, ensure NVLink topology awareness in shard allocator to minimize cross-switch hops.

3) NVIDIA L4 (Ada/Lovelace inference SKU)
- Role: cost-optimized inference for smaller models and high-QPS short responses (e.g., embeddings, short chat snippets).
- Clocking: lower-power SKU, default clocks are optimized for cost. Do not force max clocks; instead tune scheduler to use higher concurrency with smaller per-request kernels.
- Power limit: maintain default or slightly reduced caps to keep TCO low. Avoid aggressive clocking changes — L4's perf/watt profile is best left to vendor defaults for small models.
- Kernel selection: prefer int8/4-bit quantized kernels when acceptable for quality. Use smaller GEMM kernels and avoid launching very large kernels that underutilize the chip.
- Scheduling: use tight packing and higher QPS per card; use multi-instance GPU (MIG-like partitioning) if supported for isolation. Prioritize L4 for embedding endpoints and very small-context chat.
- KV cache: with smaller HBM, keep only active prefixes; aggressively evict cold KV entries. Consider a two-level cache: on-device small LRU + larger host-resident cache with async prefetch.

4) AMD MI300 (CDNA3, HBM3)
- Role: attractive for large memory footprint models and memory-bound workloads; good cost/per-token for very long context models if kernel support is optimized.
- Clocking: ROCm exposes frequency governors; prefer a sustained-high governor for inference nodes. Watch for device thermal limits and GFX frequency scaling.
- Power limit: AMD nodes often have less headroom for manual power caps; start conservative. Lowering power can have disproportionate impact on memory bandwidth-heavy workloads.
- Kernel selection: ensure ROCm kernels for matmul/attention are tuned (tuned GEMM kernels, ROCm BLAS/miopen). For long-context models prefer kernels that reduce memory traffic (fused attention + KV packing).
- Scheduling: prefer MI300 for long-context single-request workloads where memory matters more than single-thread latency. Avoid overcommitting memory-heavy models on the same GPU.
- KV cache: MI300's HBM3 is excellent for large KV sets. Keep KV on-device; use contiguous allocation patterns and align to ROCm page/segment sizes to reduce TLB/PMT overhead. If host spill required, use pinned host pages and asynchronous DMA scheduling.

Kernel selection heuristics (runtime level):
- At model registration, collect model characteristics: token-generation profile (tokens/sec), peak context bytes, typical batch sizes. Use these to tag model with kernel preference: low-latency (small-batch optimized kernels), high-throughput (large GEMM kernels), memory-bound (KV-friendly fused kernels).
- Maintain a per-node kernel benchmark cache: when a new model lands, run short kernel probes on the assigned node to select the best kernel variant (bf16 vs fp16 vs int8). Cache the result keyed by (model-arch-hypers).
- Fallback: if preferred kernel fails at runtime (OOM, kernel error), fall back to a stable reference kernel and report telemetry. Avoid automatic switch-to-experimental in production without canarying.

Scheduler placement rules (draft):
- Rule 1 (latency SLO): place latency-sensitive jobs on nodes with high sustained clocks and empty background batch queues (prefer H100 then A100).
- Rule 2 (memory SLO): place long-context models on GPUs with sufficient free HBM (prefer MI300 then H100 then A100).
- Rule 3 (cost SLO): for throughput-oriented workloads, prefer L4/A100 with packed scheduling and quantized kernels.
- Rule 4 (thermal/cluster health): prevent placing many boosted-clock nodes in the same rack if cluster thermal ceilings are close to limits.

KV cache eviction and spill policies (device-aware):
- Primary preference: keep KV shards on-device.
- Shard allocation: allocate shards so that cross-GPU NVLink/NVSwitch hops are minimized (topology-aware).
- Eviction policy: size-aware LRU with weight = (recent_access_freq * token_length). Evict shards that free most HBM with least recent access.
- Prefetch: when a request likely to access a shard not resident is accepted, asynchronously prefetch shard from host (or other GPU) while sending initial decode tokens; use speculative short-circuit to maintain tail latency.

Operational playbook (quick):
- Before enabling new clock/power policy cluster-wide: run full microbench suite overnight across representative nodes.
- Canary at 5% traffic, monitor p50/p95/p99, kernel-errors, GPU thermal events, and power draw.
- Rollout: stagger by rack/zone and watch NVLink contention for sharded KV workloads.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Quantify p95 impact across SKUs for a 10% power cap change on production workloads. (JIRA-RT-912)
- Investigate automated kernel probing that runs on cold-start model loads without adding visible latency.
- Evaluate effectiveness of a two-level KV cache for L4-heavy clusters (device LRU + host spill).
- Define telemetry signals to detect when power/clock-induced frequency scaling causes tail regressions.

Action items:
- Evelyn: wire benchmark harness to PR #842 and add scripts for KV memory-pressure tests (due 2024-12-05).
- Priya: run a controlled A100 power-cap sweep and upload results to CONFLUENCE-RT-1254 (due 2024-12-12).
- Marcus: prototype kernel-probing hook in runtime that runs non-blocking microprobes on cold model loads (WIP).

Notes and heuristics summary (copy for quick reference):
- H100 = prioritize latency, keep KV local, avoid heavy power caps in multi-tenant clusters.
- A100 = balanced, safe to modestly reduce power for consolidation.
- MI300 = prioritize memory-heavy workloads and contiguous allocation; prefer sustained-high clocks for inference.
- L4 = cost-optimized for small models; use quantization and aggressive eviction for KV.

This doc is intentionally operational and prescriptive. Do not ship cluster-wide changes without the checklist above.
